newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kidnapping stops Russian patrols in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Kidnapping stops Russian patrols in Chechnya.

text.p: Russia confined its troops to barracks in the rebel Chechnya region on Wednesday after unidentified Chechens took two of its policemen hostage, local news agencies reported.

The seizure -- which took place on Wednesday morning -- was further sign of the difficulties hampering the peace process in Chechnya, where a fragile ceasefire agreed in August has yet to lead to a permanent political settlement.
Russian military sources also said the bodies of four Russian soldiers had been found near the military airport outside the regional capital Grozny, RIA news agency said.

The policemen, from the western Siberian region of Kemerovo, were captured from one of the joint patrol with Chechen rebels which have policed the region since the August 31 deal which ended 21 months of fighting between Moscow and the separatists.
The rebels, who were unable to prevent the armed attack, immediately sent a 35-strong group to look for the hostage-takers and their captives, an official from the joint command told RIA.
The incident follows the death of 68 people -- many of them from the border troops -- in a blast in a block of flats in the southern Russian Dagestan region neighbouring Chechnya.

Rebel leaders in Chechnya have angrily denied suggestions that they were responsible for the blast. However, they said they could not rule out that go-it-alone separatist fighters were behind the explosion.
Despite such problems, efforts to further the peace process are continuing.
On Wednesday Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Russian envoy in Chechnya, Ivan Rybkin, discussed the situation in the rebel region.

Chernomyrdin is due to sign a deal regulating relations between Moscow and the region in the run-up to elections in Chechnya scheduled for January 27. It includes guarantees for tens of thousands of Russians caught up in the conflict.

But the Chechen side is insisting on a withdrawal of the remaining Russian troops in Chechnya while Moscow said this would mean a loss of control over the region, which it insists must remain within the Russian Federation.
Moscow has put forward the idea of making Chechnya, which has oil resources and a strategic oil pipeline, a free economic zone.
Hostage-taking is a common risk in the region, where the fighting, which killed tens of thousands of people, led to a total breakdown in law and order.
